stories.summary: Namibia: 'African Journalists Earn Below Basic Living Needs' 28 October 2026 New Era (Windhoek) A survey by the Federation of African Journalists (FAJ) has revealed that 61% of journalists in Africa earn below the minimum needed for basic living, raising concerns about the future of independent journalism and media freedom. The 2026 report, released on Tuesday with support from Unesco, surveyed 1 586 journalists in 45 African countries, focusing on their working conditions, labour rights, safety, and media freedom. The findings show significant economic insecurity, with 58% of respondents experiencing delayed salaries and 62% lacking written employment contracts. Additionally, 71% reported inadequate social protection, including no access to pensions or other benefits. Only 4% felt their salaries sufficiently covered essential living costs.

stories.summary: Mozambique Signs Agreement With China to Restructure Its Debt 28 October 2026 Agencia de Informacao de Mocambique (Maputo) By Alberto Massango Maputo — Mozambique's public debt with China will be restructured following the signing of a Supplementary Framework Agreement between the governments' of both countries. The agreement follows meetings held in China last April between Mozambican President Daniel Chapo and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping, in which China granted a partial forgiveness of Mozambique's debt, amounting to 204 million yuan (1.9 billion meticais) in interest-free loans that were set to mature in December 2024. The agreement was signed by the finance minister Carla Louveira and the Chinese ambassador to Mozambique Zheng Xuan. The agreement aligns with the Medium-Term Public Debt Management Strategy (2025-2029) and represents a significant step toward aligning debt repayments with the country's financial capacity, thereby strengthening the sustainability of public finances. According to Louveira, the primary impact of the agreement is the alleviation of immediate pressures on the State Budget, which allows for greater predictability in the management of public resources and creates conditions to better fund economic and social priorities.

stories.title: Africa's first Youth Olympics open in Senegal amid hope and scrutiny
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5OfLK Senegal is hoping to make Africa's historic moment count beyond the next two weeks Image: Fatma Esma Arslan Ozdel/Anadolu/IMAGO Advertisement On the final day of October, what may well be the final Summer Youth Olympics ever will begin. It will be the first on African soil as around 2,700 athletes aged 15-17 arrive in Senegal to compete across a total of 153 events in 25 sports. Hosted in eight venues across three locations – Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly, 80 kilometers (50 miles) from the capital – these Games are seen by many as a prelude to Africa hosting a full Olympics one day in the future. "I'm really excited about the Youth Olympic Games because, for the first time, I'll be representing our country," 15-year-old judoka Aisha Diop who is competing for Senegal told DW. "I am very proud to be able to represent my country at these Games. This will really motivate young African athletes because they will improve, and they will want to continue playing sports now that the Youth Games have been held here." "But this parity isn't just reflected in the overall figure. This gender parity will also be reflected in each event and in each sport where such parity actually exists." stories.title: Tanzania: Authorities Weaponize Counterterrorism Laws to Restrict Civic Space Amid Pervasive Impunity Over Violent Election Crackdown
stories.summary: Tanzania: Authorities Weaponize Counterterrorism Laws to Restrict Civic Space Amid Pervasive Impunity Over Violent Election Crackdown 28 October 2026 Amnesty International (London) Tanzanian authorities have failed to hold anyone accountable for the violence security forces inflicted on protesters, which left hundreds of people dead and thousands of others injured in the wake of the 2025 general election, Amnesty International said on the first anniversary of the crackdown. Instead of delivering justice and accountability, authorities have withheld a Commission of Inquiry report from the public and intensified attacks on civic space through the abuse of counterterrorism laws. Not a single official has been criminally investigated, let alone prosecuted and punished for the excessive force that Tanzanian security forces used against protesters. In fact, the situation has only deteriorated since the crackdown began. In a classic tactic pulled out of the authoritarian playbook, the authorities are increasingly weaponizing counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear,"Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International's Regional Director for East and Southern Africa The organization has documented how, over the past year, security agencies have committed human rights violations with impunity against government critics, opposition supporters, media organizations, and dissenting members of the ruling party.

Nigeria has taken an important step towards improving transparency in its oil and gas sector by publishing company-level greenhouse gas emissions data for the first time. The disclosure, released by the Nigeria Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (NEITI) in its 2023 oil and gas audit report , is expected to help citizens, regulators and investors understand how much pollution companies emit and whether the country is making progress towards its climate commitments. Two assailants arrived on a motorcycle and shot Yahaya Masussuka in the town of Dutsin-Ma as he was saying goodbye to visitors on Monday evening, sources told the BBC. The 47-year-old preacher and one of his guests, who was also shot, were rushed to hospital but both were pronounced dead by the attending doctor, police said. It is not clear why Masussuka was targeted, but the cleric had received death threats on social media where he posted videos in which he rejected some elements of mainstream Islam, including what happens to people after their death. It is widely believed in Islam that a person's soul will be questioned in the grave by two angels.

stories.title: Côte d'Ivoire: comment le projet «Premier continent» veut lancer un festival de cinéma et une école d'acteurs
stories.summary: Côte d'Ivoire: comment le projet «Premier continent» veut lancer un festival de cinéma et une école d'acteurs En Côte d'Ivoire, l'acteur Isaach de Bankolé et le réalisateur et producteur Philippe Lacôte se sont engagés, lundi 26 octobre, dans un projet de soutien au cinéma. Il prévoit la création d'une école de formation pour les futurs acteurs ainsi que d'un festival de cinéma à Abidjan, dont la première édition devrait voir le jour dans un an, fin 2027. Publié le : 27/10/2026 - 17:25 2 min Temps de lecture L'acteur ivoirien Isaach de Bankolé (à droite) et le Délégué général du festival de Cannes Thierry Frémaux (à gauche) échangent avec l'animateur Yves Zogbo (au cntre), au cinéma Majestic, à Abidjan, le 27 octobre 2026. © Judith Renoult/RFI Par : RFI Publicité Lire la suite Avec notre correspondante à Abidjan , Judith Renoult S'il a fait sa carrière à l'international, l'acteur ivoirien Isaach de Bankolé, qui a joué notamment dans la superproduction Black Panther , se souvient que ses premiers pas dans le cinéma ont eu lieu à Abidjan. « Dans un rayon de moins de deux kilomètres autour du quartier de mon enfance, à Treichville, s'élevaient plusieurs salles de cinéma d'envergure », rappelle-t-il. C'est donc pour soutenir l'industrie qu'il est revenu dans la capitale économique de Côte d'Ivoire pour présenter son projet, Premier continent, porté avec Philippe Lacôte, réalisateur de La nuit des rois . Le but est de créer une école de formation pour les acteurs et un festival de cinéma : « Il y a des écoles qui existent, je pense qu'il y a des structures qui forment des acteurs, mais ce qu'il faut c'est, je crois, professionnaliser le métier d'acteur. » « Professionnaliser le métier d'acteur » Isaach de Bankolé, qui a fait partie du jury du Festival de Cannes, a invité son délégué général, Thierry Frémaux, qui soutient le projet d'un rendez-vous annuel à Abidjan : « ​​​​​​​ Il en va d'un avantage mutuel, pour les professionnels du cinéma ivoirien que d'accueillir les professionnels du monde entier, et puis aussi pour les spectateurs, les critiques, les professionnels qui ne sont pas Ivoiriens de venir ici et de voir un petit peu ce qui s'y passe. » Une initiative saluée dans un secteur en plein essor, mais où il reste beaucoup à faire pour accompagner les professionnels.

stories.title: West warns of famine risk in Sudan as civil war grinds on
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, War in Sudan has led to the worst humanitarian crisis with more than 33 million people in need of assistance according to the WHO By Ondiro Oganga Published 27 October 2026 The US and 30 other Western states have warned of an "alarming deterioration" in food security in Sudan, urging the warring sides in the civil war to remove obstacles to humanitarian aid to prevent famine. In a joint statement, the signatories said conflict was the main driver of Sudan's hunger crisis, damaging critical infrastructure and disrupting food production. "There is very little to survive on," Yusuf Roble, regional director for Islamic Relief East Africa, told BBC Newsday, describing how people returning to Omdurman were finding their homes destroyed or looted. The war, which began in April 2023, has displaced 14 million people. The statement , external was signed by EU states, the UK, Canada, Switzerland and Norway, as well as the US, where it was published by the state department on Monday after first appearing on the European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations website. It estimates that 19.5 million people or 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity, including five million facing emergency levels of hunger. "I met a mother of seven children who doesn't really know the whereabouts of her husband for the last three and a half years and he was the breadwinner, the sole breadwinner for the family," Roble said.

By imposing a 3 million EGP fine, ordering the closure of Mada Masr and the seizure of its property, and detaining Lina Atallah until payment is made, the Egyptian authorities are sending a clear and ruthless message: critical, independent reporting will not be tolerated. "This draconian ruling is the culmination of years of relentless harassment and unjust proceedings designed to shut down one of the country's last remaining independent media voices. Lina Atallah should never have been prosecuted for exercising her right to freedom of expression and doing her journalistic job. The Egyptian authorities must immediately overturn this outrageous verdict, halt the forced closure of Mada Masr, and end the systematic persecution of journalists. stories.title: Paddy Donnelly obituary
stories.summary: Paddy Donnelly came to London from South Africa in the early 80s to work for the International Defence and Aid Fund for Southern Africa View image in fullscreen Paddy Donnelly came to London from South Africa in the early 80s to work for the International Defence and Aid Fund for Southern Africa Obituary Paddy Donnelly obituary My husband, Paddy Donnelly, who has died aged 70, was a South African who moved in the early 1980s to London. There he worked for the International Defence and Aid Fund for Southern Africa (IDAF), which funded the legal costs of people tried or imprisoned for anti-apartheid activity. In addition to its legal work, the IDAF had a large archive of photographs relating to apartheid, and Paddy ran that side of the operation, processing and distributing photos of ongoing state violence to media outlets, campaigning groups and many other organisations. He was an accomplished photographer himself, and many of his photos were held in the archive. He had begun by taking pictures of townships and displaced people’s camps, and when he came to the UK he photographed anti-apartheid political meetings as well as visiting or exiled South African singers, musicians and activists.

It was “now clear” that the study “will not move forward in Guinea-Bissau”, Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, a Danish researcher, wrote on LinkedIn, adding, “we were not given the necessary governmental approval.” The minister of health in Guinea-Bissau, Quinhin Nantote, previously denied that the project would move forward. “This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese last week. The study was to be funded with $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with another $1.6m from private partners like the Bill Ackman-backed Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation. “The solution is clear here: take the money and vaccinate as many kids as you can,” said Paul Offit, a vaccines expert at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, who sharply criticized the proposed study as unethical.

Flights are scheduled as early as Wednesday, according to the families and the immigration advocacy group the Workers Circle, which has been monitoring conditions and speaking with detainees inside two Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facilities in south Florida. The stunning show suggesting the future is Ghana-shaped Fondation Cartier, Paris Ibrahim Mahama put an entire factory in this exhibition exploring Ghana before and after it was ripped to shreds by colonialism. And it’s just one dazzling installation in a show full of hope Ibrahim Mahama has dug through the ruins of post-colonial Ghana, sorted through the ashes of its ancient history, picked through the industrial detritus, the corporate waste, the piles of rubbish, and found something pretty unique: hope.
